title: The Re-Engagement Script: How to Win Back "Dead" Cold Email Leads
description: How to re-engage leads who ghosted you: who to email, when, a 3-email script to copy, an AI prompt, a worked example and the mistakes to avoid.
lead: This is the full re-engagement script from the reel. You get the rules for picking which old leads to email again, the 3-email script to copy, a prompt that writes your "what changed" line, and a table of the mistakes that get re-engagement campaigns marked as spam.
insider: We follow the same rules on client campaigns: verify again, give a new reason, keep it short, and stop the moment someone says no. Steady sending like that is what produced our full quarter: **236,545 emails, a 3.69% reply rate and 1,061 interested leads** from January to March 2026. The script is the easy part. Keeping the list clean, the inboxes healthy and the follow-ups on time every week is the work we do for clients.

blocks.text: The number from the reel

One re-engagement campaign sent to **1,532 ghosted prospects got an 11.75% reply rate**. That comes from cold email operator [Christian Plascencia's post](https://x.com/coldemailchris/status/2114688513593766087), summed up by [Cold Email Daily](https://coldemaildaily.com/stories/christian-info-personal-emails-lead-every-55-contacts). 11.75% of 1,532 is about **180 replies** from people most senders had written off.

For context, [Hunter's State of Email Outreach 2026](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email) puts the average cold email reply rate at **4.5%**, and only **3%** for sales emails. So a good re-engagement campaign can beat a brand-new one. The reason is simple: these people already know your name, they fit your target, and most of them didn't say no. They just didn't answer.
Why "dead" leads usually aren't dead

items: **Timing was wrong.** They were busy, mid-project or had no budget that month. Months later, that can be different.
**Your email got buried.** A no-reply is not a no. Most people never decided anything about you.
**Their situation changed.** New boss, new funding, new hires, a new problem. People and companies change all the time.
**Your offer changed.** You may have a new result, a new service or a better price than when you first wrote.

blocks.text: Contact data also goes old fast. The [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/tenure.nr0.htm) reports that the median worker had been with their current employer **4.1 years** (January 2026). That's the middle of the range, so plenty of people move much sooner. Christian's advice in the same post is to re-check anything older than six months before you email it again.
Step 1: Pick who to re-engage (and who never to touch)
**Why:** the fastest way to hurt your domain is to email people who already asked you to stop. The fastest way to get replies is to email people who were a good fit but got the timing wrong.

head: Old lead
Re-engage?
How
rows: Wait at least 60 to 90 days after your last email, then use the script below
Write when they said to. Mention their own words: "You said Q1 might be better."
Wait 6 months or more, and only with a truly new reason
Keep them on a do-not-email list forever
Look for the person's new email, or the new person in that role
Booked a call, then went quiet
A short, human note from the person they met, not a sequence

items: Export every lead from old campaigns with their status: no reply, replied, bounced, unsubscribed.
Remove everyone who asked to stop, unsubscribed or marked you as spam. Add them to your sending tool's block list.
Remove anyone who is already in a live campaign, so nobody gets two emails at once.
Split the rest into the groups in the table above. Each group gets its own campaign.

blocks.text: Step 2: Clean the list again
**Why:** old lists bounce. Bounces tell inbox providers you're emailing strangers, and that pushes all your emails toward spam. Hunter's average bounce rate is **3.6%**. Keep yours under 2%.

items: Run the whole list through an email verifier again, even if you verified it the first time.
Remove invalid addresses. Send "risky" and catch-all addresses later, in a small separate batch.
Check that the person still has the same job. A quick look at their LinkedIn profile or the company's team page is enough for your best leads.
If they left, find who took their role. That new person is a fresh lead, and you have a good reason to write: "I used to talk with Sarah about this."

blocks.text: Step 3: Find one new reason to write
**Why:** "just checking in" gives nobody a reason to reply. A re-engagement email works when something is different from last time. That one new thing is the whole email.

head: What changed
Example line
rows: "Saw you opened a second location in Austin. Congrats."
"We just helped a company like yours book [your real number] demos."
A new offer or lower risk
"We now run a small 2-week pilot before any long contract."
"Most teams plan Q1 outreach in December. Is that true for you?"
"I made a 1-page checklist for this. Want it?"

blocks.text: Step 4: The 3-email re-engagement script
Start a **new thread with a new subject line**. The old thread is months old and may already be buried. Keep each email under 80 words, plain text, and no links in the first email.

blocks.label: Email 1 (day 1): the new reason
blocks.text:
Subject: {{first_name}}, quick update

Hi {{first_name}},

I wrote to you back in {{last_month}} about {{problem_you_solve}}. Probably bad timing.

One thing changed since then: {{what_changed}}.

Is {{problem_you_solve}} still on your list at {{company}}, or should I close the file?

{{your_name}}

blocks.label: Email 2 (day 4): give something useful
blocks.text:
Subject: Re: {{first_name}}, quick update

Hi {{first_name}},

No need to reply to the last one. I put together {{free_resource}} for {{their_role}}s at companies like {{company}}. It shows {{one_specific_thing}}.

Want me to send it over?

{{your_name}}

blocks.label: Email 3 (day 9): the polite close
blocks.text:
Subject: Re: {{first_name}}, quick update

Hi {{first_name}},

I'll stop here so I'm not cluttering your inbox.

If {{problem_you_solve}} comes up later, just reply to this email and I'll pick it up.

All the best,
{{your_name}}
A polite close often gets replies. People answer "yes, still interested" or "no thanks" because it's easy. Both answers are useful.
Step 5: Send it slowly and watch two numbers

**Why:** re-engaged lists carry more spam-complaint risk than fresh lists, because some people remember you and didn't want the first email either. [Google's sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126) ask senders to keep spam reports under 0.3%, and to aim for under 0.1%.

items: Send re-engagement emails from warmed-up inboxes that are already healthy, never from brand-new ones.
Start with your best group ("not now" replies), then add the no-reply group.
Watch **bounce rate** (under 2%) and **spam complaints** (as close to zero as you can) every day for the first week.
If someone replies "no", stop and remove them from every campaign right away.
After the 3 emails, leave the rest alone. Don't put them back into a new re-engagement round for at least 6 months.

blocks.text: Worked example
Say you have **1,500 old leads** who never replied. You re-verify the list and remove 200 bad addresses, so **1,300** are left. You send the 3-email script.

head: Reply rate
Replies from 1,300
Notes
rows: A great result, with a strong new reason

blocks.text: Math check: 1,300 × 0.03 = 39. 1,300 × 0.045 = 58.5, so about 58. 1,300 × 0.1175 = 152.75, so about 153. Even the low end is 39 conversations from a list you had given up on, and it cost you no new data.
Prompt: write your "what changed" line

blocks.label: Copy into ChatGPT or Claude
blocks.text:
You write short, plain cold emails for B2B sales.

I'm re-engaging leads who didn't reply to my emails 3+ months ago.
What I sell: [one sentence]
Who they are: [job title, industry, company size]
What changed since I last wrote: [new result / new offer / their news / new season]

Write 5 versions of one sentence that tells them what changed.
Rules: under 20 words, no hype words, no exclamation marks, sounds like a real person, no "just checking in" or "circling back".
Then pick the one you would most likely reply to and say why in one line.
Common mistakes

head: Mistake
What happens
Fix
rows: Same email, same result: no reply
Write a new email around one new reason
High bounces hurt the whole domain
Verify again before every re-engagement round
Wait 60 to 90 days after the last email
One round of 3 emails, then rest for 6+ months

blocks.text: Follow the [FTC's CAN-SPAM rules](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/can-spam-act-compliance-guide-business) in every email: honest subject line, your real business address, and a clear way to opt out that you honor quickly.

faq.q: How long should I wait before re-engaging?
faq.a: At least 60 to 90 days after your last email. For people who said "not interested", wait 6 months or more and only write if something real changed.

faq.q: Should I reply in the old thread or start a new one?
faq.a: Start a new thread with a new subject line. The old one is months old and buried. Mention the old email in one short line so it doesn't feel like a trick.

faq.q: Can I re-engage people who unsubscribed?
faq.a: No. Anyone who asked to stop stays on your do-not-email list forever.

faq.q: What if the person left the company?
faq.a: Find who took their role and email them as a new lead. Mentioning the person they replaced is a natural opener.
